one_liner: Single-header C++17 dynamic N-D R*-tree for points or boxes; matches or beats Boost.Geometry's R-tree, by up to about 35%.
what_it_does: Indexicon is a set of standalone headers (R-tree for points and for boxes, PR/pseudo-median quad-tree, MX-CIF quad-tree, oct-tree, KD-tree) with one API shape: bulk-load from an iterator range of (point or box, value) pairs, insert, remove, range query into an output iterator, kNN query and getStatistics. The R-tree is RTree<Value, Type, Dims, MaxElements = 128, ...>, with points in rtree_point.hpp and boxes in rtree_mbr.hpp. It is not a source-compatible replacement for boost::geometry::index::rtree: there are no predicate expressions, query iterators or Boost.Geometry type adaptors, and queries hand back the stored Value objects only.
how_it_is_fast: The R-tree follows the same design and defaults as Boost's rstar<MaxElements> parameters (min elements and forced-reinsert count 0.3 x capacity, overlap-cost threshold 32), and its bulk load is the same top-down packing scheme as Boost's pack_create (median counts by subtree size, nth_element along the longest edge of a hint box). The differences are in the layout and hot paths. Leaf and internal capacities are separate template parameters, and nodes keep entries in fixed inline arrays. The point tree stores raw points in leaves rather than degenerate boxes. R* splits score every split position with prefix/suffix bounding boxes in one pass per axis. A range query emits a whole subtree without per-entry tests when the query window contains the child's box.
when_to_use: Dynamic in-memory workloads mixing bulk load, inserts, deletes, range and kNN queries over tens of millions of 2D or 3D points or boxes, which is what the README charts measure (3.5M to 112.8M records)

You already use Boost's R*-tree and want the same algorithm with about 10-20% less insertion time at large capacities (256-512) and about 15-35% less range-query time at small capacities, without a Boost dependency
Projects that want a single dependency-free header and compile-time dimension, coordinate type and node capacities, including more than 3 dimensions
Research or teaching code that compares several index families (R-tree, quad-tree, MX-CIF, oct-tree, KD-tree) behind one API
when_not_to_use: You need Boost's query language (intersects/within/covered_by/nearest predicates and their combinations), query iterators, or adapting your own geometry types
Static data queried far more than it changes: packed static indexes such as GeoToolbox KdBoxTree or a Hilbert-packed R-tree avoid insert machinery entirely
Production code that needs maturity: 17 commits, a repo created in May 2026, no tests beyond usage examples, and no published benchmark harness
Insertion-heavy workloads where the gap matters: the gain over Boost is small (parity at capacities 32-64 on OSM and MIAMI), while PH-tree reports about 5x faster inserts than Boost

integration.platforms: any platform with a C++17 compiler; no SIMD or OS-specific code in the R-tree headers
integration.thread_safety: not documented. query, queryPoint and knnQuery are const and keep no internal mutable state, so concurrent reads look safe; insert and remove need external locking
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same R*-tree parameter set and packing algorithm as boost::geometry::index::rtree<..., rstar<N>>, but a different API (insert(point, value), query(box, out_iter), knnQuery(point, k, out_iter)), no predicates, and no allocator parameter

gotchas: Both R-tree headers put `using namespace std;` at global scope and define RPoint, RBox, Node, RTree, contains and intersects in the global namespace, so rtree_point.hpp and rtree_mbr.hpp cannot be included in the same translation unit and may clash with your own names
RTree owns raw node pointers and deletes them in its destructor but neither deletes nor defines copy or move operations, so copying a tree (for example, passing it by value) double-frees
knnQuery writes the k results in heap order, not sorted by distance, and k = 0 calls front() on an empty vector (undefined behavior)
Each node is a fixed std::array of capacity + 1 entries (default capacity 128), so sparse nodes still occupy full size. remove() needs an exact coordinate match plus Value ==
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over PH-tree or tidwall/rtree.c when you want a classic R*-tree that behaves like Boost's (same parameters and packing) in arbitrary dimensions, as one dependency-free header. Pick PH-tree for much larger insert gains, tidwall/rtree.c for a plain C 2D dynamic tree, and GeoToolbox KdBoxTree or nanoflann for static data.
verified_claims_summary: Two first-party README charts compare Indexicon's R-tree with Boost.Geometry's R-tree on six real datasets (MARINE, MIAMI, OSM, TAXIS, TIGER, TORONTO; 3.5M-112.8M points or boxes, 2D and 3D) at node capacities 32-512. Indexicon is at or below Boost at every plotted point: insertion is about 20% lower at capacity 512 (MARINE about 25 s vs 31.8 s) and range queries about 34% lower at capacity 32 (MARINE about 280 ms vs 425 ms), all values read off the images (derived from page data). Neither the Boost balancing algorithm (linear, quadratic or rstar), compiler flags, CPU nor the query workload is stated, and the Boost harness is not in the repo; the companion arXiv paper 2606.04676 (same authors) could not be opened from this environment.
status_note: New, active academic project (MIT, 25 stars, 17 commits, last commit 2026-08-17). Its one GitHub issue, which questioned the fairness of the paper's dynamic-tree vs nanoflann comparison, was closed with no reply shown. Small enough to vendor, but treat it as research-grade code.
